facts.title: CodeGraph: Pre-indexed code knowledge graph for coding agents (colbymchenry/codegraph)
facts.event_hint: CodeGraph: local-first Rust-native code knowledge graph MCP server for coding agents
facts.problem: AI agents discover code structure the slow way: grep, glob, and Read one file at a time, manually rebuilding call paths and dependencies. This generates a large pile of tool calls and network round-trips before the agent can start the actual task. On large or tangled codebases, a strong model without an index burns millions of tokens re-deriving structure that a pre-built graph already contains.
facts.mechanism: CodeGraph is a local-first tool (npm CLI + MCP server) that builds a pre-indexed semantic code knowledge graph from a codebase and serves it to agents. Extraction: a native Rust kernel parses 20+ languages using tree-sitter grammars compiled into it, extracting nodes (functions, classes, methods) and edges (calls, imports, extends, implements). Resolution: function calls resolve to definitions, imports to source files, class inheritance links, and framework-specific routing patterns (17 web frameworks). Storage: local SQLite database (.codegraph/codegraph.db) with FTS5 full-text search. Auto-sync: native OS file events (FSEvents/inotify/ReadDirectoryChangesW) with 2-second debounce trigger incremental sync of only changed files; per-file staleness banners during the debounce window warn the agent to Read directly. Connect-time catch-up reconciles (size, mtime) + content-hash against the working tree. Cross-language bridging: Swift<->ObjC (@objc auto-bridging), React Native legacy bridge + TurboModules + Fabric, Expo Modules, native->JS event emitters — edges tagged provenance:'heuristic'. MCP exposes a single codegraph_explore tool that returns verbatim source, call paths (including dynamic-dispatch hops), and blast-radius summary. Framework-aware routes link URL patterns to handler classes/functions.

evidence.claim: Benchmark across 7 real-world repos and 7 languages: 89% fewer tool calls, 60% cheaper, 69% fewer tokens, file reads cut to zero on all seven repos
evidence.value: 89% fewer tool calls; 0 file reads WITH CodeGraph
evidence.condition: Claude Opus 4.8 headless, --strict-mcp-config, WITH = CodeGraph MCP enabled, WITHOUT = empty MCP config; 4 runs per arm, median reported; one architecture-understanding question per repo

evidence.claim: Per-repo results: VS Code (~11k files TS) 2 vs 40 tool calls, 83% fewer tokens, 75% cheaper; Tokio Rust (~790 files) 3 vs 57 tool calls, 91% fewer tokens, 86% cheaper; Django Python (~3k) 2 vs 29 tool calls, 78% fewer tokens, 69% cheaper
evidence.value: 2 tool calls / 0 file reads (VS Code WITH CodeGraph)
evidence.baseline: 40 tool calls / 17 file reads (VS Code WITHOUT)
evidence.condition: Same architecture question ('How does the extension host communicate with the main process?'); median of 4 runs

evidence.claim: Indexing speed: Swift compiler repo (27k files) fresh-indexes in ~100 seconds; Linux kernel (70k files, 2M symbols, 6.4M relationships) indexes in under 12 minutes on a 2-core/6GB VPS
evidence.source_locator: 'Built for speed — the Rust kernel' section
evidence.value: ~100s for 27k-file Swift repo; <12 min for 70k-file Linux kernel
evidence.condition: Worker pools, parallel resolution, and analysis caches sized from actual system resources (container/cgroup-aware core counts, measured available RAM)

evidence.claim: Incremental sync: saving a file updates the graph in well under a second; watcher fires 300ms after a lone save, syncs ~0.3s of work on a 4,400-file project and ~0.4s on the 27,000-file Swift compiler repo
evidence.source_locator: Auto-sync description in 'Built for speed' and 'How It Works' sections
evidence.value: ~0.3s sync time for one-file change on 4,400-file project
evidence.condition: Measured against fastest competing indexer across 31-repo, 30-language benchmark; gap widens with repo size because CodeGraph cost grows with the change, not the repository

evidence.claim: Cross-file coverage measured per language on benchmark repos: TypeScript 95.8%, Python 100%, Go 96.6%, Rust 86.7%, Java 93.3%, C 92.2%, Swift 95.3%, Kotlin 96.2%
evidence.condition: Coverage = share of symbol-bearing source files with at least one resolved cross-file dependent; residual is genuine static-analysis frontier (runtime dispatch, reflection/DI, framework conventions, vendored code)

facts.evaluation_context: 7 real-world open-source codebases: VS Code (TS, ~11k files), Excalidraw (TS, ~640), Django (Python, ~3k), Tokio (Rust, ~790), OkHttp (Java, ~645), Gin (Go, ~110), Alamofire (Swift, ~110). Agent: Claude Opus 4.8 run headlessly (claude -p). Config: --strict-mcp-config, WITH arm has CodeGraph MCP + built-in Read/Grep/Bash, WITHOUT arm has empty MCP config + built-in Read/Grep/Bash. 4 runs per arm, median reported. Questions are single architecture-understanding queries per repo. Cost = total_cost_usd; Tokens = total tokens (input incl. cached + output); Time = wall-clock; Tool calls = every tool invocation including sub-agents. Repos cloned at --depth 1.
facts.limitations: Benchmark is self-conducted by the tool author — not peer-reviewed and not compared against competing academic systems (RepoGraph, CodeNib, etc.) in the same benchmark. Only architecture-understanding questions tested — no issue resolution, patch generation, multi-step coding, or SWE-bench evaluation. The 89%/60%/69% aggregates are medians across diverse repos; per-repo variance is large (token savings range from 18% on Gin to 91% on Tokio). Time metric is noisy: on 2 small repos (Excalidraw, Alamofire) the WITHOUT arm finishes wall-clock faster while spending 5-10x more tokens. Cross-language bridges use heuristics with provenance tags — accuracy of Swift<->ObjC, RN bridge edges not independently validated. Coverage is measured on one benchmark repo per language — not a population estimate. The ~64.5k stars claim (from discovery summary) is not visible in the README and cannot be verified. No information about memory consumption of the graph at scale or query latency distributions.
facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses project question 2 (whether code knowledge graphs reduce real task latency). CodeGraph represents the production/tooling end of the code-graph spectrum vs. CodeNib's research-system end. Key contrasts: (1) CodeGraph uses a single SQLite graph + FTS5; CodeNib uses separate lexical/dense/structural views with explicit validity boundaries. (2) CodeGraph claims 89% fewer tool calls and 0 file reads on architecture questions; CodeNib reports 50-87% fewer trajectory tokens on localization. (3) CodeGraph's auto-sync (watcher + debounce + staleness banner) is a production-grade freshness solution; CodeNib's incremental maintenance is measured against independent rebuilds with strict exact-match checks. (4) CodeGraph's benchmark is self-conducted on easy-to-verify architecture questions; CodeNib's is on SWE-bench-derived localization with rigorous statistics. For the briefing, CodeGraph demonstrates that the code-graph approach has reached production maturity (native Rust kernel, 20+ languages, cross-language bridging, framework-aware routing) and delivers measurable agent acceleration in its targeted use case. The open question is whether these gains transfer to harder tasks (issue resolution, patch generation) where the agent must also write and verify code, not just understand architecture.
